# AIDID

> AIDID is a zero-backend, quantum-safe login protocol for third-party websites.
> A user proves control of a `did:msg` DID by signing one canonical message with a
> CRYSTALS-Dilithium-5 key that never leaves the user's own device. An integrator adds
> an RP-side SDK call and one chain read; there is no AIDID server in the loop.
> The protocol, the RP SDK and a fully offline end-to-end demo are implemented.
> Production login is NOT available yet — see the status document below.

## Read this first (machine-readable)

- [Full text](https://aidid.im/llms-full.txt): everything below in one fetch — the onboarding guide, the spec index and every wire format.
- [Schemas index](https://aidid.im/schemas/index.json): every machine-readable contract, with its spec document, spec version and sha256.
- [Status](https://aidid.im/status.json): what works today, what is blocked, and the agent-identity policy.
- [Registry](https://aidid.im/registry.json): third-party sites that have proven control of their origin. This file is generated with the deployment; the live view the site itself reads is https://registry.aidid.im/registry.json — a first-party cache of the public repository, refreshed on demand (there is no fixed schedule), with the generated file as the offline fallback.
- [Submit to the registry](https://github.com/imAiDID/aidid-registry): open a pull request that adds one entry to `rp-registry.json`. A GitHub Action fetches `https://<origin>/.well-known/aidid-rp.txt` and auto-merges when it matches, **including pull requests opened from a fork** — no invitation or collaborator access is needed; the free pull-request channel is transitional until the on-chain registry (0.01 MSG per registration) becomes available. A merge needs no rebuild to become visible: the directory page reads the first-party cache above and falls back to the generated file. A verified entry proves control of the origin — not security or reputation.
- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/index.json): the SDK and prose-spec bundles, with byte length, sha256 and SRI.
- [Login SDK tarball](https://aidid.im/download/aidid-login-0.1.0.tgz): `npm install` this directly — no registry account needed.
- [Login request schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-request.schema.json): the request an RP generates.
- [Login response schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-response.schema.json): what the wallet returns.
- [Sign-in message schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-message.schema.json): the exact canonical text that is signed.
- [Sitemap](https://aidid.im/sitemap.xml): the human-facing pages that actually exist.

## Getting started

- [Tutorial index (machine-readable)](https://aidid.im/start/index.json): the five journeys with their full English and Chinese text and a per-step status that matches status.json — the twin of the human pages below.
- [Start here](https://aidid.im/start/): the five journeys as human pages, each step badged as available today, offline-testable today, or not available today.
- [Get a DID](https://aidid.im/start/did/): a specification walkthrough only — creating a DID costs MSG and there is no end-user path to obtain MSG yet, so this is not a working sign-up.
- [Delegate a sub-DID](https://aidid.im/start/subdid/): rehearse the whole parent-to-child flow offline today; on-chain binding, revocation and quota are blocked.
- [Integrate AIDID login](https://aidid.im/start/integrate/): the five-minute quick start (copy-paste code to install the SDK, generate a request, verify the callback fail-closed and mount the drop-in button), plus the same-device vs cross-device transports and a go-live checklist; production login is blocked until the chain-side resolve endpoint is authorised.
- [Use DID login for payments](https://aidid.im/start/pay/): resolve the DID on your server and read the payout address from the canonical record; `resources: ['pay:address']` is a declaration the user sees, the response carries no address, and reading a real address in production is blocked.
- [Back up and restore](https://aidid.im/start/backup/): works today and runs entirely in the browser; there is no server-side recovery.
- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/): the SDK and prose-spec bundles with install commands, byte length, sha256 and SRI, and how to verify a file.

## How a third party integrates AIDID login

1. Read the wire contract — `signin-request`, `signin-response`, `signin-message`,
   `login-error` — from the [schemas index](https://aidid.im/schemas/index.json).
2. Generate the request on your server: type `auth`, version `1.0`, `chainId`
   `msg-chain-1`, a single-use `nonce` of at least 16 characters, and a 5-minute TTL.
   Present it as a QR code or hand it out as a `web+aidid://auth?payload=…` deeplink.
3. The user's wallet builds and signs the canonical sign-in message on the user's own
   device. The Dilithium-5 private key never reaches your site.
4. The response comes back in the callback URL fragment (`<uri>#response=…`). Verify it
   against the request YOU stored — never against the request echoed in the response.
5. Use the published `@aidid/login` package — its source lives at `frontend/packages/aidid-login-sdk` in the
   (private) repository, but you do not need the repository: install it from
   https://aidid.im/download/aidid-login-0.1.0.tgz and use
   `createSignInRequest` / `verifySignInResponse`. `@aidid/login/callback`
   (`readResponseFromLocation` / `parseResponseFragment`) reads the callback fragment and
   `@aidid/login/widget` (`mountSignInButton`) renders the drop-in button, so a ten-line
   integration is enough. Self-test with `examples/node/offline-demo.mjs` from the same tarball — it runs
   offline with real Dilithium-5 signing. The full copy-paste quick start is at
   https://aidid.im/start/integrate/ (see also https://aidid.im/start/pay/ for the payout-address flow).

## What an AI agent can and cannot do here

- It **can** read every contract on this site, write an RP-side integration, and run the
  offline demo (no network, no chain, real signatures).
- It **can** hold its own `did:msg` — but only as a sub-DID delegated from a parent DID,
  where the parent DID holder is the responsible party. Agents do not get independent key
  material. See `agentIdentity` in [status.json](https://aidid.im/status.json).
- It **cannot** sign in on a user's behalf. That signature requires the user's own
  Dilithium-5 key or passphrase, and AIDID never asks anyone to hand it over.

## Honest limits

- The chain-side DID resolve endpoint is not authorized yet, so no DID can be resolved in production.
- There is currently no end-user path to obtain MSG in order to create a DID.
- VC issuance and on-chain anchoring are designed but not implemented.
- Chain write paths await the chain-side window parameters; mainnet is No-Go.

## Optional

- Authoritative prose specs (v1): download https://aidid.im/download/aidid-specs-v1.tgz — in the (private)
  repository they live at `docs/specs/` at the repository root, one level above `frontend/`.
- Behavioral test vector with a real signature: `frontend/packages/aidid-login-sdk/fixtures/offline-signin-vector.json`
  (also inside the SDK tarball as `package/fixtures/offline-signin-vector.json`).

## Onboarding guide

Tutorials as data: the human pages under /start/ and this section are generated from the same source.
Machine-readable twin (both English and Chinese text, per-step status): https://aidid.im/start/index.json
Step status vocabulary: available (works today) | offline-testable (write and self-test now, cannot run in production yet) | blocked (not available today; refs names the unavailable capabilities in status.json).

### 1. Get a DID (status: blocked; refs: userCreatesDid)

Human page: https://aidid.im/start/did/

A DID is a did:msg identity registered on MSGChain. Creating one needs MSG to pay the chain fee, and there is no end-user way to obtain MSG yet, so read this as a specification walkthrough rather than a working sign-up.

#### did-1 — What a DID is (status: available)

A DID is an identifier of the form did:msg:<suffix>. Its document holds a controller, one or more verification methods, and an authentication list.

AIDID uses CRYSTALS-Dilithium-5 (round-3) keys: public key 2592 bytes, signature 4595 bytes. The private key never leaves the user's device; a login is one signature over a canonical text message.

The shapes are frozen in machine-readable schemas, so read did-document, msg-did and canonical-resolve in the schemas index before writing any code.

- [Schemas index](https://aidid.im/schemas/index.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### did-2 — Registering a DID needs MSG, and no user can get MSG today (status: blocked; refs: userCreatesDid)

Registering a DID is a chain write (register_did on the chain's DID registry) that costs a chain fee paid in the native umsg denomination.

There is no public faucet and no end-user path to obtain MSG. An ordinary user therefore cannot create a DID, and the login chain starts broken; this is recorded as the unavailable capability userCreatesDid in status.json.

Do not build a sign-up flow that assumes the user already holds a DID and MSG. The honest status today is fail-closed.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)
- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/)

#### did-3 — Chain writes wait for the window parameters (status: blocked; refs: chainWrite)

Any chain write, including DID registration, update and deactivation, or deploying the identity contract, is blocked until MSGChain releases its window parameters. Mainnet is No-Go and no contract is deployed; the blocked capability is chainWrite.

What you can do today instead: design against the specs and the JSON Schemas, and rehearse everything that does not need a chain in the offline demo.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)
- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/)

### 2. Delegate a sub-DID (parent to child) (status: offline-testable; refs: offlineEndToEnd)

Human page: https://aidid.im/start/subdid/

A parent DID can authorise a restricted-scope sub-DID for a purpose, a resource set and a validity period, and bind an AI agent to it. You can rehearse the whole flow offline today; on-chain binding, revocation and quota need stage B and the window parameters.

#### subdid-1 — What a sub-DID is: a restricted-scope grant, not a separate key (status: available)

A sub-DID is a did:msg whose document has controller: [<parent DID>] and an AididDelegation service entry carrying the grant payload: purpose, resource scope, expiry, bound agent and status.

In stage A the child document reuses the parent's Dilithium-5 key material: its verification method points at the parent public key. So this is a hand-off of restricted permissions, not a hand-off of keys. Never describe it as giving an agent its own production key.

The own-key mode, where the parent signs over the agent's own Dilithium-5 public key, exists at the protocol level and is verifiable offline, but it is fail-closed by default and has no on-chain binding or revocation.

- [Delegation payload schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/delegation/delegation-payload.schema.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### subdid-2 — Create it locally and run the offline demo (status: offline-testable; refs: offlineEndToEnd)

The offline demo in the RP SDK (examples/node/offline-demo.mjs, section 6) walks the whole flow with real Dilithium-5 signatures and no network: create a sub-DID, have the parent sign the delegation, sign in as the sub-DID (all 11 login checks pass), let the delegation gate allow it, have an out-of-scope resource refused, verify the audit receipt, and finally revoke and watch the identity still verify while the login is refused with delegation_revoked.

Install the published SDK and run the same demo from the tarball if you do not have the repository.

- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/)
- [Downloads index](https://aidid.im/download/index.json)

#### subdid-3 — Verify a sub-DID on the RP side (step 12, fail-closed) (status: offline-testable; refs: offlineEndToEnd)

RP verification reuses the 11 login checks and adds step 12: read the delegation entries from the resolved child document (no entry means reject with delegation_not_found), then evaluate the payload for scope, expiry and expected parent.

The SDK ships verifyDelegation and createDelegationVerifier. It never throws and never downgrades to allow. It needs one of two trust sources: the on-chain child document, or the parent's signature over the canonical delegation text. For own-key payloads it rejects unless the caller explicitly opts in with allowOwnKey: true, because there is no revocation channel offline.

It does not count quota or run a deny-list. scope.maxUsesPerDay is declared metadata only, so counting, rate limiting and deny-lists are the RP's own responsibility.

- [Delegation payload schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/delegation/delegation-payload.schema.json)
- [Delegation error codes](https://aidid.im/schemas/delegation/delegation-error.schema.json)

#### subdid-4 — What is still blocked: on-chain binding, revocation and quota (status: blocked; refs: chainWrite, independentAgentKey)

There is no on-chain authoritative binding of a sub-DID to an agent, no revocation primitive (the chain's deactivate is irreversible and there is no blacklist), and no enforced quota. Those need stage B, our identity contract, which is written but not deployed until the window parameters are released. Stage A writes the grant into the child DID document through the chain's own registry contract, and that write is blocked today too.

Until then, treat every sub-DID grant as a local arrangement that can only be revoked by updating the document, and keep the honest wording: restricted-scope authorisation, not an independent production key.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

### 3. Integrate AIDID login into your site (status: offline-testable; refs: rpIntegration, offlineEndToEnd)

Human page: https://aidid.im/start/integrate/

Write and self-test the RP-side integration today, entirely offline: read the wire contract, install the SDK, build a request, verify a response, and run the offline end-to-end demo. Production login is blocked until the chain-side resolve endpoint is authorised.

#### integrate-1 — Five-minute quick start (1/4): install the SDK (status: available)

The SDK is served as a static file from this site: no npm account, no registry account and no backend of ours in the loop. The package is pure ESM.

Only the signature verifier imports the optional peer @msg-chain/sdk (the Dilithium-5 primitive). Message building, request and response verification, the callback reader and the drop-in button are dependency-free, so they also run inside an edge worker.

- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/)
- [Downloads index](https://aidid.im/download/index.json)

#### integrate-2 — Five-minute quick start (2/4): generate the request on your server (status: available; refs: rpIntegration)

createSignInRequest fills type, version, an https uri default, a single-use nonce (32 CSPRNG bytes) and a 5-minute expirationTime. Keep the TTL at or below 5 minutes.

Store the request yourself: the response only echoes it back, and that echo proves nothing. The web entry point is https://aidid.im/authorize/?payload=... and that URL must not change.

- [Sign-in request schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-request.schema.json)
- [Wallet entry point](https://aidid.im/authorize/)

#### integrate-3 — Five-minute quick start (3/4): verify the callback, fail-closed (status: offline-testable; refs: rpIntegration, offlineEndToEnd)

The eleven ordered checks run inside verifySignInResponse. It returns { ok: false, error } and never downgrades to allow.

Today it always fails closed at the resolve step with endpoint_unavailable, because the chain-side resolve endpoint is not authorised. That is the honest result, not a bug in your code. nonces must be a shared store (Redis, D1, a Durable Object), not createMemoryNonceStore, as soon as you run more than one instance.

- [Login error codes](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/login-error.schema.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### integrate-4 — Five-minute quick start (4/4): mount the drop-in button (status: available; refs: rpIntegration)

The widget renders a plain button with an inline SVG and no hosted asset, so there is nothing to style or fetch. On creation it reads #response= once (the wallet returns to request.uri#response=...), clears it from the address bar, then calls onResponse exactly once — or onError with a stable reason (no_fragment is not an error).

It does not verify anything and never approves silently, and it never puts /authorize in an iframe. Verification stays on your server.

- [Sign-in request schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-request.schema.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### integrate-5 — Two transports: same device (top-level redirect) vs cross device (QR / deeplink) (status: available; refs: rpIntegration)

mode: 'auto' picks redirect when a browser exists and the device looks like the one holding the DID (a mobile user agent, including iPadOS reporting a macOS UA), otherwise deeplink. The auto rule is specified in SPEC-LOGIN-v1 §9.2 (a user-agent / touch-point heuristic), and it stays a heuristic: pass mode explicitly when you know your audience better than the heuristic does.

Same device: a top-level navigation to the wallet. After the user approves, the wallet returns to your callback URL with #response=..., and the widget reads that fragment.

Cross device: the widget shows a web+aidid://auth?payload=... string and a copy button; render the QR with your own library, because the SDK ships no QR dependency. The phone that holds the DID approves and lands on your callback page — the browser on the other machine does not see the response by itself. Today the spec defines no server-side handoff, so the callback page must POST the fragment to your server and the originating browser must poll for the resulting session.

Not verified on hardware: whether an iOS PWA (display: standalone) returns to the RP automatically after approval has not been tested on a real device. Test it in your own target environment and offer a fallback (for example a link the user can open manually).

- [Wallet entry point](https://aidid.im/authorize/)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### integrate-6 — Read the wire contract first (status: available)

The RP contract is four machine-readable schemas: signin-request (what you generate), signin-message (the canonical text that gets signed), signin-response (what the wallet returns) and login-error (the stable error strings you must handle).

The prose authority is the login specification, shipped in the specs tarball. Read section 0 (honest limits) and section 7 (the eleven ordered checks) before writing code.

- [Schemas index](https://aidid.im/schemas/index.json)
- [Downloads index](https://aidid.im/download/index.json)

#### integrate-7 — Run the offline end-to-end demo (real signatures, no chain) (status: offline-testable; refs: offlineEndToEnd)

The fixture uses a fixed public test seed to derive a Dilithium-5 key pair and signs the canonical message for real. It exercises request, approve, verify and session with no network, no chain and no testnet.

Three runnable paths: the Node flow (examples/node/offline-demo.mjs from the tarball), the browser flow against the SDK's browser bundle, and a server-side example that shows verifySignInResponse plus an HTTP resolver, which fails closed with endpoint_unavailable when no public endpoint exists.

The demo does not check chain state, because a fixture resolver replaces canonical resolve, so it cannot prove that a DID exists on chain. Its test key must never be used for a real identity.

- [Downloads](https://aidid.im/download/)
- [Downloads index](https://aidid.im/download/index.json)

#### integrate-8 — Verify responses in eleven ordered steps, fail-closed (status: offline-testable; refs: rpIntegration, offlineEndToEnd)

Verify in order and reject on the first failure: parse the response; compare nonce and domain with your stored request; rebuild the canonical message and compare byte-for-byte; check expiry; consume the nonce once; check the chain id; resolve the DID on the server; confirm the verification method is in authentication; allow only the Dilithium-5 proof type; verify the signature; then create the session.

Resolve must be server-side, because the agent API returns no CORS headers and a browser cannot call it. There is no built-in rate limit and no Retry-After, so cache with a 5 to 15 second TTL, use single-flight, back off on failure, and do not batch. Consume the nonce before verifying the signature.

The bridge proof type AididP384BridgeSignature2025 is demo-only; reject it unless you explicitly opt in, and label it non-quantum-safe if you do.

- [Login error codes](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/login-error.schema.json)
- [Canonical message schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-message.schema.json)

#### integrate-9 — Go-live checklist: do not ship before every line is true (status: offline-testable; refs: rpIntegration, offlineEndToEnd)

Before production, all of these must hold:

1. The chain-side resolve endpoint is authorised. It is not today (didLoginProduction), so every real verification fails closed with endpoint_unavailable.
2. The signing user actually holds a DID. Most users cannot create one today, because there is no end-user path to obtain MSG (userCreatesDid).
3. Your nonce store is shared across instances and consumes a nonce atomically; a per-instance memory store will accept replays.
4. Resolve runs server-side with a 5 to 15 second TTL cache and single-flight; the API has no CORS and no built-in rate limit.
5. You handle every stable error from login-error (did_not_found, did_deactivated, nonce_replayed, endpoint_unavailable, and the rest) and never fall back to an anonymous session.
6. Registering in the directory is optional and is only a declaration that you control your origin. It is not a security endorsement and it is not required to log in.

Until items 1 and 2 are true, ship nothing that claims to be a working sign-in.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)
- [Login error codes](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/login-error.schema.json)

#### integrate-10 — Production login is blocked (chain-side resolve not authorised) (status: blocked; refs: didLoginProduction)

You can finish and self-test the integration, but you cannot go live: GET {agent_api}/agent/v1/aidid/resolve is not authorised on the public network yet, so an RP cannot resolve any DID in production. This is the unavailable capability didLoginProduction in status.json.

Do not describe AIDID login as production-ready, and do not ship a flow that silently falls back to an anonymous session when resolution fails. The correct behaviour is fail-closed with endpoint_unavailable.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### integrate-11 — List your site in the registry (proof of origin, nothing more) (status: available)

Once your integration is written you can publish /.well-known/aidid-rp.txt on your origin and open a pull request against the public registry repository. A GitHub Action fetches your file and compares it with the registered challenge; a pull request that changes only the registry file and matches is merged automatically — including a pull request opened from your own fork, with no invitation or collaborator access needed. Registration is free and explicitly transitional until the on-chain registry exists.

There is no rebuild to wait for: the directory page reads a first-party cache that is refreshed on demand (a cache older than ten minutes triggers a refresh, rate-limited to once every ten minutes), and falls back to the snapshot built into the deployment when that read fails — so a merged entry normally shows up on your next visit or two.

Being listed proves only that you control the origin and declare the integration. It is not a security or reputation endorsement by AIDID.

- [Third-party registry](https://aidid.im/registry/)

### 4. Use DID login for payments (payout address) (status: offline-testable; refs: rpIntegration, offlineEndToEnd)

Human page: https://aidid.im/start/pay/

After a verified login you can resolve the DID on your server and read the payout address from the canonical record. You can write and self-test that logic offline today; reading a real address in production is blocked with the rest of production login. pay:address is a declaration the user sees and approves, not a permission.

#### pay-1 — Where the payout address actually comes from (status: available)

A login response carries a did, a canonical message and a signature — no account address. To get the address you resolve the DID and read the canonical record on the server.

The record field owner is the 44-character MSG account address (msg + 40 hex + one checksum digit). The document's controller field is different: it lists controller DIDs, not addresses, so never send MSG to a did:msg:... string. Check deactivated before you use the address, and do not cache it longer than your resolve TTL (5 to 15 seconds); a name-to-address mapping can change between DID updates.

- [Canonical resolve schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/did/canonical-resolve.schema.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### pay-2 — resources: ['pay:address'] is a declaration, not a grant (status: available)

Adding pay:address to resources puts a statement into the canonical message that the user signs, and the wallet shows it on the approval page: "this site will obtain your payout address". It is a declaration, and the protocol says so explicitly.

It is not a permission, it grants no on-chain right, and it does not mean the user authorised a payment. The response still contains no address, so you must resolve the DID yourself. If you do not request pay:address, do not derive, display or use the address for payment at all.

- [Sign-in request schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/login/signin-request.schema.json)
- [Wallet entry point](https://aidid.im/authorize/)

#### pay-3 — Binding the address to the DID: keys, devices and sub-DIDs (status: offline-testable; refs: offlineEndToEnd)

The address belongs to the DID, so the questions that matter are about the DID and where it lives.

New device or restored backup: a restore brings back the same DID document, so the same owner address still applies. A newly created DID gets a new address, so never hard-code an address against a user account.

Key rotation or a DID update: re-resolve before every payout; the record carries a monotonic version and an updated block time, and the owner can change across updates.

Sub-DIDs: a sub-DID is its own did:msg with its own resolve record. Pay the sub-DID's owner only when that sub-DID is the identity you accepted, and remember that a sub-DID grant has no on-chain revocation channel today — a revoked grant may still resolve until the document is updated.

Deactivated DIDs: refuse before reading an address (did_deactivated), and keep your own deny list, because the chain has no blacklist.

- [Canonical resolve schema](https://aidid.im/schemas/did/canonical-resolve.schema.json)
- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

#### pay-4 — Today: offline self-test yes, production address no (status: blocked; refs: didLoginProduction)

Everything above can be written and self-tested offline today, with a fixture resolver in place of canonical resolve: the request, the approval declaration, the callback, the resolve step and the address read.

What you cannot do today is read a real address in production. Resolve is not authorised on the public network, so the address step fails closed with endpoint_unavailable for every DID. Do not ship a checkout or payout flow that depends on it; the honest status is fail-closed until the chain side authorises the endpoint and ordinary users can actually hold a DID.

- [Capability status](https://aidid.im/status.json)

### 5. Back up and restore your local identity (status: available)

Human page: https://aidid.im/start/backup/

Backup and restore work today and are entirely local: the payload is encrypted with a passphrase that never leaves your device. There is no server-side recovery, so the backup and its passphrase are the only way to move an identity to another device.

#### backup-1 — Why you must back up: there is no server-side recovery (status: available)

Your signing key is stored passphrase-encrypted in this browser. AIDID has no backend and holds no copy, so there is no recovery link and no support reset: if you forget the passphrase you must create a new identity.

That is why the backup is the migration path. Keep the exported carrier and its passphrase somewhere safe. The passphrase is not stored inside the carrier, so losing it means the backup cannot be decrypted by anyone.

- [Home (backup panel)](https://aidid.im/)

#### backup-2 — What the backup contains, and what it does not (status: available)

Every carrier wraps the same payload: your DID document, your Dilithium-5 key material, your credentials, your sub-DID grants and your sub-DID usage receipts.

It deliberately excludes your local visited-sites footprint and the backup UI preference. Nothing identity-related lives in IndexedDB, sessionStorage or the service-worker cache.

- [Home (backup panel)](https://aidid.im/)
- [Sub-DID records](https://aidid.im/identities/)

#### backup-3 — Choose a carrier (status: available)

Open Backup / Restore on the home page, enter a passphrase of at least 8 characters, then export. Carriers: a CKX text string, a .ckx file, a PNG image, a video carrier, or the legacy .encrypted.json. Restore accepts paste, a file picker and drag-and-drop.

A PNG only survives a byte-for-byte copy: a screenshot, or any chat-app recompression or resize, destroys the hidden payload. A video carrier is appended to a source video you choose (keep it under 64 MB) and the result still plays normally. CKX carriers are optional; the JSON path works on its own.

- [Home (backup panel)](https://aidid.im/)

#### backup-4 — Restore semantics: an old backup never wipes your sub-DID records (status: available)

Sub-DID grants and usage receipts are optional members of the payload, and their import semantics are deliberately asymmetric.

If the member is missing or is not an array, restore leaves your existing local records untouched: an old backup that predates sub-DIDs must not silently delete the only copy of a grant. If the member is an array, including an empty array, it is treated as authoritative and replaces the local table wholesale. Malformed entries are filtered by the same validators the storage layer uses.

Restoring a backup that contains a stale chain mirror can overwrite a newer local cache; the chain copy can always be re-fetched.

- [Home (backup panel)](https://aidid.im/)
- [Sub-DID records](https://aidid.im/identities/)

#### backup-5 — If a restore fails, read the message (status: available)

Restore distinguishes four cases before decrypting: not a valid AIDID backup (empty or not a carrier at all), carrier damaged or truncated, unsupported CKX format version, and wrong passphrase or corrupted backup. A structure check runs before the expensive key derivation, so junk input fails fast and nothing is written.

A failed restore is fail-closed: your current local state is left unchanged.

- [Home (backup panel)](https://aidid.im/)
